title: White Boy Rick
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck discuss the true story of White Boy Rick (Richard Wershe Jr.), who was recruited as an off-the-books FBI informant in 1984 at age fourteen while living on Detroit's East Side. They cover his role informing on the Curry brothers' drug organization and its ties to Detroit City Hall and police, his brief shooting, the FBI's dropping him in 1986, his later wholesale cocaine dealing, his 1987 arrests, his life sentence under Michigan's 650-Lifer Law, Operation Backbone from prison, repeated parole denials, his 2017 release, and later legal and documentary efforts. The episode also includes a Stuff at Sea cruise promotion and a brief sign-off.

entities.name: Tommy Hearns vs. Marvin Hagler fight

segments.title: Show open
segments.summary: Opening credits and announcement of the episode topic.

segments.title: Opening banter on White Boy Rick
segments.summary: Hosts introduce White Boy Rick, mention the Matthew McConaughey film and documentaries, and frame the story as a true account of a teen FBI informant caught up in the War on Drugs.

segments.title: Family background and East Detroit in the 1980s
segments.summary: Rick Wershe Jr. grows up on Detroit's East Side as white flight and crack spread. His father, Richard Wershe Sr., is a gun store manager and hustler whose FBI customers become the link to the later informant work. Rick learns street hustling, including house break-ins, and the Chamber Brothers dominate the local crack trade.

segments.title: Terrence Bell and the first FBI contact
segments.summary: Older associates including Terrence Bell teach Rick crime skills. At fourteen he shoots at men who stole a family car. In spring 1984, FBI agents visit the Wershe house with photos, and Rick starts identifying people, which prompts the FBI to recruit him.

segments.title: Curry twins and Detroit city hall connections
segments.summary: Rick names the Curry twins, Johnny (Little Man) and Leo (Big Man), as the main East Side drug figures. Johnny Curry was married to Kathy Vulson, niece of Mayor Coleman Young. Homicide commander Gil Hill is described as deeply tied to the drug trade. Detroit's homicide count is cited as very high at the time.

segments.title: Gil Hill and recruitment as an off-the-books informant
segments.summary: Hosts describe Gil Hill's role as the Beverly Hills Cop character and his payoffs. The FBI proposes making fourteen-year-old Rick an informant; his father agrees to be listed as the nominal informant. Rick befriends Rudell Curry, who nicknames or is associated with the name White Boy Rick, and he gets into the Curry gang's world.

segments.title: Rick's role inside the Curry gang
segments.summary: Rick is trusted in high-level Curry gang meetings and gathers information for the FBI. The FBI pays him around thirty thousand dollars over the first couple of years, and he buys cars, a fur coat, and a Rolex.

segments.title: Money, cars, and the teen's perspective
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the money Rick earned, comparing it with their own teen jobs, and how the FBI-funded lifestyle pushed him into a dangerous world. They note his father did not stop him and was involved in his life.

segments.title: Shooting, Operation raid, and Las Vegas trip
segments.summary: In November 1984 Rick is shot in the stomach by a gang member, and gang members take him in a car before an ambulance intervenes. The FBI persuades him to continue. In February 1985 a raid based on his information yields about two hundred thousand dollars, cocaine, and guns. FBI agent John Anthony calls him the most productive informant in Detroit. The FBI pays for him to attend a Marvin Hagler vs. Tommy Hearns fight in Las Vegas with Detroit dealers.

segments.title: Damian Lucas killing and cover-up
segments.summary: A drive-by shooting by the Curry gang accidentally kills thirteen-year-old Damian Lucas. Police drop the investigation, and Johnny Curry is said to have paid a bribe to cover it up. Rick overhears Johnny Curry speaking with Gil Hill about the cover-up. The FBI cuts ties with Rick in June 1986, shortly before he turns sixteen.

segments.title: Rick's own drug career and wholesale cocaine
segments.summary: After the FBI drops him, Rick enters the real drug trade, reportedly already underway during his informant work. He buys large quantities of cocaine from Art Derek, a Miami-linked wholesaler, acting as a weight man. He remains an associate of the Curries rather than a Curry soldier. The Chamber Brothers are described as making large sums selling crack.

segments.title: Curry indictments and Gil Hill hit attempt
segments.summary: The Curry twins are indicted in 1987 and plead guilty to drug and racketeering charges. Hosts say Gil Hill offered Nate Boonecraft one hundred twenty-five thousand dollars to kill Rick. Boonecraft later admitted trying twice.

segments.title: Relationship with Kathy Vulson
segments.summary: Rick, around seventeen and earning about thirty thousand dollars a month, starts dating Kathy Vulson, who is older. Hosts say the relationship gave him status and that Detroit police were ordered to watch over her.

segments.title: May and October 1987 arrests
segments.summary: On May 22, 1987, Detroit police arrest Rick, finding thirty thousand dollars and eight keys of cocaine stashed under a neighbor's porch. He posts bail and is arrested again in October with five kilos of cocaine and guns, some found at his father's and grandparents' houses. The media begin national coverage of White Boy Rick, with Chris Hansen accused of inflating his importance.

segments.title: Trial and media portrayal
segments.summary: Federal officials offer Rick a chance to testify against others, which he declines. The trial does not disclose his informant status. Hosts describe a media org chart presenting him as a kingpin. Rick later claims the public defenders were connected to the mayor, a claim not proven.

segments.title: Life sentence under the 650 Lifer Law
segments.summary: At seventeen Rick is sentenced to life without parole under Michigan's 650-Lifer Law for possessing 650 grams or more of cocaine. The judge says he is worse than a mass murderer, and says she had no choice. The governor later calls the law his greatest mistake. Matthew McConaughey gives interviews about his son's FBI work.

segments.title: Operation Backbone and Florida transfer
segments.summary: From prison in 1991, Rick helps the FBI in Operation Backbone, using Kathy Vulson's prison visits to introduce an undercover agent. The operation leads to eleven cops being charged, including Mayor Young's inner circle; Kathy Vulson's charges are dropped. Rick is moved to a Florida prison under a new name, but is later charged with running a car theft ring from prison, leading to a 2005 racketeering conviction.

segments.title: Parole denials and later informant recognition
segments.summary: Johnny Curry is released in 1999 after seventeen years and cooperates. Parole is denied to Rick in 2003, 2008, and 2012, with Detroit police officers opposing him in 2003. Greg Schwartz writes a letter supporting him. Seth Ferranti's 2013 column and Evan Hughes's 2015 Atavist article bring the story to wider attention. Rick misses his father's funeral.

segments.title: Sentence overturned, release, and lawsuit
segments.summary: Judge Dana Hathaway throws out the life sentence, prosecutors appeal and win, and Rick is granted parole after thirteen more years and released in 2017 at forty-seven. He is later returned to Florida custody on the earlier sentence and released in July 2020. A lawsuit against the federal government is dismissed because the statute of limitations had run out.

segments.title: Documentary project and hosts' aside
segments.summary: Hosts mention Rick's documentary project with director Hype Williams, and Chuck says he worked with Hype Williams. The hosts transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Stuff at Sea cruise promotion
segments.summary: Promotion for the Stuff at Sea voyage aboard Virgin Voyages from New York City to Bermuda, October 2 through 7, with live shows.

segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to send email to the show's address.

segments.summary: Standard iHeartRadio closing credit directing listeners to the app and podcast platforms.
